# 1 Line and Texture

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Line

A **line** is a mark or stroke made with pen, pencil, paint or similar, to show
movement, an object's placement, or to communicate a visual feeling.

Depending on how line is used in a composition, the artist can use it to
communicate a specific emotion. This is the practical point of the unit: the
direction of a line carries meaning before any subject is recognised.

| Line | Communicates |
|---|---|
| **Vertical** | Stability, structure, power |
| **Horizontal** | Rest, relaxation, calmness |
| **Curving** | Movement, sporadic, energy |
| **Diagonal** | Unbalanced, chaotic |

**Contour** is the outline — the edge or line that defines or bounds a shape or
object. Objects would not be visible to the human eye without a contour:

- In a **two-dimensional** drawing or painting, the contour lines can be
  considered the object's outline
- In a **real, three-dimensional** object, the contour is simply the line that
  defines its edges

An **implied line** is a line that does not physically exist but is implied to
exist.

## Texture

**Texture** is a visual characteristic of the relationship between the way an
object looks and the way it feels to touch. **Visual texture** is used in art to
communicate an idea or emotion.

## Composition and its devices

**Composition** is a visual characteristic of the relationship between the way an
object looks and feels.

**Overlap** is when an object covers or partially covers another object in a
composition, to convey the idea of space. Overlapping helps communicate **depth
and a sense of real space**.

**Repetition** is when something is repeated or occurs over and over again within
the same composition. Using repetition helps give a composition **unity and
consistency**.

## Artists

| Artist | Known for |
|---|---|
| **Edgar Degas** | A French artist famous for his paintings, sculptures, prints and drawings |
| **Andy Warhol** | An American artist, director and producer; a leading figure in the visual art movement known as **pop art** |
| **Henri Matisse** | A French artist known for his use of colour and his fluid, original draughtsmanship. A draughtsman, printmaker and sculptor, but known primarily as a painter |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Line** | A mark or stroke made to show movement, an object's placement, or a visual feeling |
| **Contour** | The outline; the edge or line that defines or bounds a shape or object |
| **Implied line** | A line that does not physically exist but is implied to exist |
| **Texture** | The visual characteristic of the relationship between how an object looks and how it feels |
| **Composition** | The visual characteristic of the relationship between the way an object looks and feels |
| **Overlap** | When an object covers or partially covers another to convey space, communicating depth |
| **Repetition** | When something recurs in a composition, giving it unity and consistency |
| **Pop art** | The visual art movement in which Andy Warhol was a leading figure |

# 2 Colour and Value

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Colour (hue)

**Colour**, or **hue**, is the amount of light reflected on an object. The only
way an object's colour can be seen depends on the amount of light reflected from
its surface.

1. **Primary colours** — natural or basic colours that cannot be created by
   combining other colours
2. **Secondary colours** — the combination of two primary colours
3. **Tertiary colours** — the combination of a primary colour and a secondary
   colour

The three build on one another in order, which is why the wheel has the structure
the schemes below depend on.

## Value (tint, tone and shade)

**Value** is the degree of lightness or darkness within a given colour, shade,
tone or tint. Changing a colour's value usually makes the colour seem **less
intense or subtle**.

| Term | Added | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Shade** | Black | The value becomes darker with the degree of shade used |
| **Tone** | Grey | The value becomes greyer with the degree of tone used |
| **Tint** | White | The value becomes lighter with the degree of tint used |

## Colour schemes

| Scheme | Definition | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Monochromatic** (单色模式) | A wide range of tints and shades of a single colour | Harmonious and subtle |
| **Complementary** (互补色模式) | Opposite colours on the colour wheel | Very vibrant |
| **Analogous** (相似色模式) | A set of colours adjacent to each other on the colour wheel | Harmonious and subtle |
| **Split complementary** (补色分割模式) | A combination of complementary and analogous schemes, allowing intensity but not as strong as pure complementary | Vibrant and harmonious |
| **Triadic** (三等分配色模式) | Three colours equally spaced around the colour wheel | Vibrant and harmonious |

## Balance

**Balance** is arranging elements in a composition so that no one part of a work
overpowers or seems heavier than any other part. It is a **principle of design**
dealing with the **visual weight** within a composition.

- **Symmetrical** — a balance showing stability, usually centred in the composition
- **Vertical** — a type of symmetrical balance with a vertical orientation
- **Horizontal** — a type of symmetrical balance with a horizontal orientation
- **Asymmetrical** — a balance that is neither centred nor symmetrical
- **Radial** — a balance where all the elements expand or spiral out from a
  central point

## Focal point, contrast and intensity

The **focal point** is the focus, or most important visual part, within a
composition. The basic elements and principles help determine it — for example
the way implied line is used, colour and value intensity, and contrast.

**Contrast** is the difference or opposition between two objects or elements. It
is a principle of design: the arrangement of opposite elements — light against
dark colours, rough against smooth textures, large against small shapes — to
create visual interest.

**Intensity** is the strength or sharpness of a colour, due to its degree of
freedom from mixture with its complement. A colour's intensity is seen at its
**purest form**, when not mixed with any other colour, shade, tone or tint. Other
factors also affect it, such as a change of value around a specific colour, or
the texture around a given colour.

Note how the three connect: contrast and intensity are both ways of directing the
eye, and both are among the means of establishing a focal point.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Colour (hue)** | The amount of light reflected on an object |
| **Primary colours** | Basic colours that cannot be created by combining others |
| **Secondary colours** | The combination of two primary colours |
| **Tertiary colours** | The combination of a primary and a secondary colour |
| **Value** | The degree of lightness or darkness within a colour, shade, tone or tint |
| **Shade** | Black added to a colour, darkening its value |
| **Tone** | Grey added to a colour, making its value greyer |
| **Tint** | White added to a colour, lightening its value |
| **Monochromatic** | A wide range of tints and shades of a single colour |
| **Complementary** | Opposite colours on the colour wheel |
| **Analogous** | Colours adjacent to each other on the colour wheel |
| **Split complementary** | Complementary and analogous schemes combined |
| **Triadic** | Three colours equally spaced around the colour wheel |
| **Balance** | Arranging elements so no part overpowers or seems heavier than another |
| **Symmetrical** | Balance showing stability, usually centred |
| **Asymmetrical** | Balance that is neither centred nor symmetrical |
| **Radial** | Balance in which elements expand or spiral out from a central point |
| **Focal point** | The most important visual part within a composition |
| **Contrast** | The arrangement of opposite elements to create visual interest |
| **Intensity** | The strength or sharpness of a colour, from its freedom from mixture with its complement |

# 3 Elements and Principles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Shape

A **shape** is a two-dimensional area created when a line or contour is closed,
when there is a change in value, or through some other form of contrast.

Shapes help create complex drawings and paintings, affect composition, and
contribute to the balance within a work. **All shapes are two-dimensional**,
meaning they have only length and width — which is exactly what distinguishes
shape from form below.

- **Geometric shapes** are usually recognisable by name, and mathematics can be
  used to find information about them: circle, square, trapezoid
- **Organic shapes** seem to follow no rules
- **Tessellation** is an arrangement of shapes closely fitted together,
  especially polygons in a repeated pattern without gaps or overlapping

## Form

**Form** is an element of art similar to shape but with the added dimension of
**depth**.

## Movement and pattern

**Movement** is a principle of design that uses any element to show energy, flow,
or a feeling that objects within a composition are in motion.

**Pattern** is showing consistency with colours, lines, values and textures
throughout a composition.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Shape** | A two-dimensional area created when a line or contour closes, when value changes, or through contrast |
| **Geometric shape** | A shape usually recognisable by name, about which mathematics can give information |
| **Organic shape** | A shape that seems to follow no rules |
| **Tessellation** | Shapes closely fitted together in a repeated pattern without gaps or overlapping |
| **Form** | An element of art like shape, but with the added dimension of depth |
| **Movement** | A principle of design using any element to show energy, flow, or objects in motion |
| **Pattern** | Consistency of colours, lines, values and textures throughout a composition |

# 4 Inner Space and Perspective

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Space

**Space** is the visual element referring to the area between, around, above,
below and within objects. It gives artwork its dimension and helps communicate
**dynamic composition**. Sometimes the space is not actually within a piece — only
the **illusion** of it is.

**Negative space** is the space surrounding shapes or forms in two- and
three-dimensional art. It acts as a balance to positive space, is often
overlooked, and gives the eye **a place to rest**, increasing a composition's
appeal through subtle means.

**Positive space** is the area or part of a composition that the subject occupies
— the composition's actual **subject matter**, the main focus of a work. Its
specific elements render detail to catch the viewer's eye, and it should work
**equally with negative space**.

That last point is why negative space is treated as an element at all rather than
as leftover background.

## Proportion and foreshortening

**Proportion** is a principle of art describing the **size, location or amount of
one element in relation to another**, or to the whole — the relationship between
the sizes of figures and objects within a composition. For example the size of an
arm in relation to the rest of the body, or the size of a person in relation to
the size of a house.

**Foreshortening** is a method of rendering a specific object or figure in depth.
The artist records the **distortion seen by the eye** when an object or figure is
viewed at a distance or at an unusual angle.

## Perspective

**Perspective** was developed in the **15th century** by the architects **Leon
Battista Alberti (1404–72)** and **Filippo Brunelleschi (1377–1446)**. It remained
one of the basic principles of Western art until it was challenged by the ideas of
the **Cubists** at the start of the 20th century.

Two kinds are distinguished:

- **Linear perspective** deals with the organisation of shapes in space
- **Atmospheric or aerial perspective** deals with atmospheric effects on tones
  and colours

### One-point perspective

The perspective of a rectangle or box. It uses a **single vanishing point** to
draw an object, and is the **simplest** form of perspective drawing.

- The **front and back transversal planes always remain parallel to the picture
  plane**
- Only their **scale changes** as an object recedes into the distance
- Only the **receding orthogonal lines change angles**

There are **two types of construction line** used in perspective drawing.

### Two-point perspective

Used in illustrations of objects that have been **rotated at an angle to the
picture plane**. It uses **two sets of orthogonal lines and two vanishing points**
to draw each object, and there are **no longer any planes parallel to the picture
plane**.

The difference between the two follows from that last line: rotating the object
removes the parallel plane, and a second vanishing point is needed to place the
edges that are now receding.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Space** | The visual element referring to the area between, around, above, below and within objects |
| **Negative space** | The space surrounding shapes or forms, balancing positive space and giving the eye a place to rest |
| **Positive space** | The area a composition's subject occupies; its actual subject matter |
| **Proportion** | The size, location or amount of one element in relation to another or to the whole |
| **Foreshortening** | Rendering an object in depth by recording the distortion the eye sees at a distance or unusual angle |
| **Perspective** | The 15th-century principle developed by Alberti and Brunelleschi, challenged by the Cubists |
| **Linear perspective** | Perspective dealing with the organisation of shapes in space |
| **Atmospheric perspective** | Perspective dealing with atmospheric effects on tones and colours |
| **One-point perspective** | The simplest form, using a single vanishing point, with front and back planes parallel to the picture plane |
| **Two-point perspective** | Perspective for objects rotated to the picture plane, using two vanishing points and no parallel planes |
| **Vanishing point** | The point to which receding lines converge |
| **Orthogonal lines** | The receding lines that change angle as an object recedes |

# 5 Vocabulary of Art and Architecture

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

This unit is a vocabulary list. The terms are grouped here by what they describe,
which is not how the guide orders them, so that related terms sit together — the
definitions themselves are the guide's own.

## Techniques and materials

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Fresco** | Plaster wall paintings |
| **Tempera** | A water-based pigment mixed with egg yolk |
| **Mosaics** | The use of small coloured objects to form a larger image |
| **Illumination** | Coloured illustrations containing gold and silver |
| **Printmaking** | The art of using different techniques to make prints |
| **Camera obscura** | A dark box or room with a small opening to let light in |

## Handling of light and detail

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Chiaroscuro** | Extreme contrast of dark and light values |
| **Tenebrism** | Exaggerated contrast of darks and lights |
| **Realism** | Attention to extreme detail |
| **Symbolism** | The use of an object to represent a meaning other than its own outward appearance |

Chiaroscuro and tenebrism are close: both name a contrast of dark against light,
tenebrism being the more exaggerated of the two.

## Figures and arrangement

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Contrapposto** | Counterpose; used to describe a body gesture where one leg is in front of the other |
| **Isocephaly** | Arranging the heads of figures at the same level |

## Formats of panel painting

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Diptych** | Two panels of artwork hinged together |
| **Triptych** | Three panels of artwork hinged together |
| **Polyptych** | A painting with more than three panels hinged together |

The three differ only by panel count, which makes them easy to confuse and easy
to ask about.

## Architecture

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Columns** | A post or structure used to support an architecture |
| **Arch** | A curved architectural element used to span an opening |
| **Vault** | The use of the Roman arch with a depth added to it |
| **Flying buttress** | Flying arches combined with tower buttresses |
| **Rotunda** | Architecture with a round structure and a dome at the top |
| **Cathedral** | A large Romanesque or Gothic style church that houses the chair (*cathedra*) of the Bishop |
| **Cruciform** | Any design in the shape of a cross |
| **Chateaux** | A French castle or large country house |

## Religion, patronage and style

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Icon** | Religious symbol |
| **Patron** | A person who supports the arts |
| **Rococo** | Late Baroque style, described as pretty or overdone |

# 7 Movements from Neoclassicism to Primitivism

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The movements run in rough sequence, and several are defined by what they reject
in the one before.

## Neoclassicism

**Neoclassicism** literally means *the New Classic Period*. **Napoleon's interest
in the Classical Greek and Roman periods** resulted in his idea to **relive** those
periods.

**Allegorical** means symbols that tell a story — a symbolic narrative. Most of
**David's** works both told a story, mostly historical, and carried some symbolic
meaning or parallel to what was happening in modern-day France.

## Romanticism

**Romanticism** was a movement with a **revival of interest in Medieval stories and
the emotion of artistic elements**.

**Nonobjective** art is art that has **no recognisable subject matter, only the use
of raw elements**. Some artists in Romantic art used **non-representational subject
matter** to communicate the emotion of an idea.

## Realism

A **Realist** is an artist who painted in the Realist movement. The Realists
emphasised the **depiction of the common, everyday world** — a direct turn away from
Romanticism's medieval subjects.

## Photography

**Photography** is the art of producing images on **photosensitive**, or
light-sensitive, paper. The technology came from the idea of **printmaking** and how
an image can be made by first creating a mould or stencil.

## Impressionism and Pointillism

**Impressionism** is a style of painting emphasising **momentary effects of light on
colour**. Artists sought to create an **instant impression, not a detailed
analysis** — which is the direct opposite of Realism's attention to extreme detail.

**Pointillism** is colours **systematically applied to canvas with small dots**.
The guide notes we see a similar technique today in TV screens, computers and
colour printing.

## Expressionism

**Expressionism** is the **communication of strong personal and emotional feelings**
in artwork. **Van Gogh** was considered the artist who began this movement.

## Primitivism

**Primitivism** is the **less sophisticated native art of any culture**. **Gauguin**
moved to **Tahiti** because he became interested in a much more primitive lifestyle.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Neoclassicism** | Literally the New Classic Period; Napoleon's interest in Classical Greece and Rome led to his idea of reliving those periods |
| **Allegorical** | Symbols that tell a story; a symbolic narrative |
| **Romanticism** | A movement reviving interest in Medieval stories and the emotion of artistic elements |
| **Nonobjective** | Art with no recognisable subject matter, using only raw elements |
| **Realist** | An artist painting in the Realist movement, emphasising the common, everyday world |
| **Photography** | The art of producing images on photosensitive paper |
| **Impressionism** | A style emphasising momentary effects of light on colour, seeking an instant impression rather than detailed analysis |
| **Pointillism** | Colours systematically applied to canvas with small dots |
| **Expressionism** | The communication of strong personal and emotional feelings in artwork, begun by Van Gogh |
| **Primitivism** | The less sophisticated native art of any culture |
